title: High-temperature Superconductors
lead: A superconductor carries current with no resistance at all, but only when it is cold enough. This section defines the critical temperature, follows the ceramics found since 1986 that superconduct at far higher temperatures, and weighs the reports of still higher ones that will not reproduce.
objectives: Discuss the need for a high-T<sub>c</sub> superconductor.
summary_html:
• High-temperature superconductors are materials that become superconducting at temperatures well above a few kelvin.
  • The critical temperature $\kTempc$ is the temperature below which a material is superconducting.
  • Some high-temperature superconductors have verified $\kTempc$s above 125 K, and there are reports of $\kTempc$s as high as 250 K.

figures.original_caption: A graph of resistivity versus temperature for a superconductor shows a sharp transition to zero at the critical temperature T_c. High temperature superconductors have verifiable T_c s greater than 125 K, well above the easily achieved 77-K temperature of liquid nitrogen.

(a) This graph, adapted from an article in Physics Today, shows the behavior of a single sample of a high-temperature superconductor in three different trials. In one case the sample exhibited a T_c of about 230 K, whereas in the others it did not become superconducting at all. The lack of reproducibility is typical of forefront experiments and prohibits definitive conclusions. (b) This colorful diagram shows the complex but systematic nature of the lattice structure of a high-temperature superconducting ceramic. (credit: en:Cadmium, Wikimedia Commons)

exercises.prompt: What is critical temperature $T_{\text{c}}$? Do all materials have a critical temperature? Explain why or why not.

answer.solution: The critical temperature $T_{\text{c}}$ is the temperature at which and below which a material becomes a superconductor, its resistivity dropping to zero. Not all materials have one. Superconductivity happens only in materials whose electrons can couple and travel through the material without losing energy to it, and many materials never do this however cold they are made: good conductors such as copper, silver and gold have never been made superconducting, and neither have most insulators. A material with no superconducting state has no critical temperature at all; the resistivity of such a metal falls as it is cooled but levels off at a small value that is not zero.

exercises.prompt: Explain how good thermal contact with liquid nitrogen can keep objects at a temperature of 77 K (liquid nitrogen’s boiling point at atmospheric pressure).

answer.solution: Heat leaking into the object from its warmer surroundings flows on into the liquid nitrogen, as long as the two are in good thermal contact. Liquid nitrogen at its boiling point cannot get any warmer at atmospheric pressure: the heat it receives goes into vaporizing it, as latent heat, rather than raising its temperature. So the nitrogen stays at 77 K while it boils away, and an object in good contact with it is held at 77 K as well, because any heat that would warm the object is carried off into the boiling liquid. The object stays at 77 K for as long as some liquid nitrogen remains to be boiled.

exercises.prompt: Not only is liquid nitrogen a cheaper coolant than liquid helium, its boiling point is higher (77 K vs. 4.2 K). How does higher temperature help lower the cost of cooling a material? Explain in terms of the rate of heat transfer being related to the temperature difference between the sample and its surroundings.

answer.solution: Heat leaks into a cold sample from its room-temperature surroundings at a rate proportional to the temperature difference between them, as in conduction, $Q/t = kA(T_{2}-T_{1})/d$. A sample at 77 K differs from a room at 293 K by 216 K, while one at 4.2 K differs by about 289 K, so with the same insulation less heat leaks into the warmer sample each second. Every joule that leaks in must be removed, by boiling away coolant or by running a refrigerator, so less heat leaking in means less coolant used and less work done. Removing heat at a higher temperature is also cheaper in itself: the best coefficient of performance of a refrigerator, $T_{\text{c}}/(T_{\text{h}}-T_{\text{c}})$ for its cold and hot reservoirs, is $77/216 = 0.36$ at 77 K but only $4.2/289 = 0.015$ at 4.2 K, so each joule removed at 4.2 K costs about 25 times as much work.

exercises.prompt: A section of superconducting wire carries a current of 100 A and requires 1.00 L of liquid nitrogen per hour to keep it below its critical temperature. For it to be economically advantageous to use a superconducting wire, the cost of cooling the wire must be less than the cost of energy lost to heat in the wire. Assume that the cost of liquid nitrogen is $0.30 per liter, and that electric energy costs $0.10 per kW·h. What is the resistance of a normal wire that costs as much in wasted electric energy as the cost of liquid nitrogen for the superconductor?

answer.hint: In one hour the nitrogen costs $0.30, which buys 3.0 kW·h of electric energy, so the normal wire may waste 3.0 kW. Find the resistance that dissipates this power at 100 A from $P = I^{2}R$.
